top.line: Agents, fragile infrastructure and spreadsheet risk are colliding
top.para: A first draft of a conference talk argues three problems arrive at once: agents as the insider threat that never scaled, infrastructure designed for none of it, and risk management on spreadsheets at quarterly speed. Together they leave companies blind and slow. The way out carries an irony: constraining an agent lets you trust it with more autonomy.

s0.line: Three known problems combine into one insider scenario
s0.para: Agents are reasoning engines with tools and skills, harmful even without malice. Infrastructure lacks journals, unified identity and least privilege, and fails on its own, as the largest cloud outages showed. Risk management on spreadsheets cannot see reach, so it cannot fund controls and the plug gets pulled. Brakes are what let a car go fast.

s1.line: An agent is an insider with every skill
s1.para: Human and code insiders were bounded by hours, conscience or static logic; an agent is a model in a loop with tools and every skill. Incidents include Replit deleting a production database, Gemini CLI destroying files, Amazon Q's injected wipe prompt, EchoLeak, and an espionage campaign where Claude did 80 to 90 per cent of the work.

s2.line: Business infrastructure cannot recover, identify or contain agents
s2.para: Four gaps: no journaling and daily backups, unmanaged non-human identity, permissions that are the union of everything (workloads use under 5 per cent of grants), and fragile containment, shown by the fourteen-hour AWS DNS outage and Cloudflare's configuration failure. Zero-days like ToolShell dissolve controls, and internal systems lack adversarial antibodies.

s3.line: Spreadsheet risk management decides too slowly to fund controls
s3.para: 48 per cent of organisations track risk in spreadsheets, reviewed quarterly, when agent decisions need seconds and pre-approved envelopes. Without seeing reach, nobody can judge appetite or fund controls. Gartner predicts over 40 per cent of agentic projects cancelled by 2027; the plug comes out when nobody can stop or recover.

s4.line: Agent incidents go unseen because nobody has to report
s4.para: Aviation's confidential reporting system takes about 100,000 reports a year, 1.8 million so far, protected from use against the reporter. Cyber has nothing similar: CIRCIA's final rule slipped to September 2026. Verizon's 2025 report shows the human element in about 60 per cent of breaches, and the unreported column is likely worse.

s5.line: Together they form one nightmare already in the record
s5.para: An entity acting as employee, user and API at machine speed, infrastructure that cannot stop it or replay to before, and a decision process that sees nothing until a spreadsheet row afterwards. Every piece is in eighteen months of public record, just reported separately as different kinds of news.

s6.line: Constraining agents is what lets you grant them autonomy
s6.para: The way out: write down reach, mandate, gap and barriers in an Agent Behaviour Policy, where only a boundary is a control. Contain in layers with identity per agent and journaling twins, watch in real time, decide in advance through a licence to operate and expiring risk acceptance, and prove provenance. Brakes make speed survivable.

s7.line: A forty-minute talk in three acts and a turn
s7.para: The proposed talk runs three acts: the insider, the infrastructure and the spreadsheet, then turns to disclosure and the way out. It would take forty minutes, one figure per act with sourced evidence, aimed at security conferences, risk and audit audiences, and boards. Organisers are asked which act they want more of.

s8.line: Sources: the reports, incidents and studies cited
s8.para: Sources include Ponemon's 2025 Cost of Insider Risks, Anthropic's agent and espionage reports, Simon Willison's lethal trifecta, the Replit, Gemini CLI, Amazon Q and EchoLeak incidents, CyberArk, Microsoft, AWS and Cloudflare outage analyses, Gartner, MIT NANDA, NASA ASRS, CIRCIA and Verizon's 2025 DBIR.
